hard.q: «Mevrouw Peeters, ___ bent nieuw in Gent, toch?»
hard.e: Con mevrouw (una signora che non conosci bene) si usa la forma di cortesia u, con il verbo di jij: u bent. jij avrebbe il verbo giusto ma è troppo confidenziale.
hard.tt: Signora Peeters, Lei è nuova a Gand, vero?

hard.q: Het boek en de tafel zijn nieuw. → ___ zijn nieuw.
hard.e: Per più cose si usa sempre ze, qualunque sia l'articolo: una het-parola più una de-parola fanno comunque ze.

g.ze: loro / essi (anche per le cose al plurale)
g.hij: lui / esso (solo una de-parola al singolare)

hard.tt: Il libro e il tavolo sono nuovi. → Sono nuovi.

hard.q: Anna en ik komen uit Italië, maar ___ wonen nu in Antwerpen.
a: we
wij
hard.e: Anna + io = noi: we o wij, con il verbo al plurale (wonen). Non lasciarti ingannare da Anna en ik: il pronome giusto non è ik né ze.
hard.tt: Anna e io veniamo dall'Italia, ma ora abitiamo ad Anversa.

hard.q: Meneer Claes, ___ u ook uit Brussel?
a: bent
hard.e: Con u il verbo zijn è come con jij: u bent, mai u is.
hard.tt: Signor Claes, anche Lei è di Bruxelles?

hard.q: Voi abitate a Bruges, ma noi abitiamo a Gand.
a: Jullie wonen in Brugge, maar wij wonen in Gent
Jullie wonen in Brugge, maar we wonen in Gent
Jullie wonen in Brugge maar wij wonen in Gent
Jullie wonen in Brugge maar we wonen in Gent
hard.e: jullie e wij vogliono il verbo al plurale: wonen. Con il contrasto suona meglio la forma accentata wij. Brugge = Bruges.

hard.q: Lei (Anna) è la mia amica e abita a Gand.
a: Zij is mijn vriendin en ze woont in Gent
Zij is mijn vriendin en zij woont in Gent
Ze is mijn vriendin en ze woont in Gent
Ze is mijn vriendin en zij woont in Gent
Zij is mijn vriendin en woont in Gent
Ze is mijn vriendin en woont in Gent
hard.e: zij/ze + is (singolare) = lei. Dopo en puoi ripetere il pronome oppure ometterlo, perché il soggetto è lo stesso: è uno dei pochi casi in cui il soggetto può mancare.

hard.q: Lui abita a Bruges, ma lei viene da Anversa.
hard.a: Hij woont in Brugge maar ze komt uit Antwerpen
hard.e: Due frasi, ognuna con il suo soggetto: hij woont … ze komt uit. Il verbo resta al singolare.
hard.tt: Lui abita a Bruges, ma lei viene da Anversa.

hard.q: Voi siete stanchi, ma noi no.
hard.a: Jullie zijn moe maar wij niet
hard.e: jullie zijn (plurale). Nel contrasto maar wij niet la persona è accentata, quindi serve la forma forte wij: maar we niet non si dice.
hard.tt: Voi siete stanchi, ma noi no.

en.note:
The idea

Subject pronouns are the words that tell you who does the action: I, you, he… Good news: just like in English, the subject is always required in Dutch. You say Ik woon in Gent (I live in Ghent), never just Woon in Gent. The tricky part for English speakers is elsewhere: Dutch has three words for "you", and "it" is not always het.

The table

Englishstressedunstressed
Iik('k)
you (informal)jijje
you (formal)uu
hehij(ie)
shezijze
it (thing)het('t)
wewijwe
you (plural)julliejullie
theyzijze

The forms in brackets are heard in fast speech, but you don't need to use them yourself.

Stressed or unstressed?

Many pronouns have two forms. The unstressed one (je, ze, we) is the normal one: it's what you hear most. The stressed form (jij, zij, wij) is used when you want to highlight the person, usually for a contrast: Jij bent moe, ik niet (YOU are tired, I'm not). In English you'd just say the word louder; Dutch changes the word. If in doubt, both are correct.

Three kinds of "you"

jij/je is for friends, family and people your age. u is the polite form, for people you don't know well, and it works for one person or several. Watch out: with u the verb takes the same form as with jij (u bent, u woont). jullie is the informal plural "you" (like "you guys" or "y'all") and takes a plural verb (jullie zijn).

Zij: she or they?

zij/ze means both "she" and "they". The verb tells you which: zij is = she is, zij zijn = they are.

For things: hij or het

English uses "it" for every thing. In Dutch, when you refer to a thing already mentioned, the pronoun depends on the noun's article (more on this in unit 3). With a noun that takes de you use hij: de tafel → hij. With a noun that takes het you use het: het boek → het. In the plural it's always ze. So to a Dutch speaker, a table is a "he".

Watch out: typical mistakes for English speakers

  • Capitalizing ik like English "I": in the middle of a sentence it's ik, lowercase.
  • Using het for every "it": De tafel? Het is groot → Hij is groot.
  • Using the "he/she" verb with u: u is → u bent.
en.vlaams: In informal Flemish speech you'll often hear gij/ge instead of jij/je: "Waar woont ge?". In writing and with people you don't know, use u, which is more widespread in Belgium than in the Netherlands: many children even use it with their grandparents.

drills.e: Things with de become hij (in Belgium, feminine nouns like de stad become ze instead).

g.ze: they, or she for feminine nouns

drills.e: With u the verb is the same as with jij: u bent.

items.q: You're talking to your new boss in Brussels. Which pronoun do you use?
items.e: u is the polite form, singular and plural.

a: ik
items.e: ik = I. Unlike English 'I', it's written lowercase (except at the start of a sentence).

a: jullie

items.q: Het boek is nieuw. → ___ is nieuw.
De tafel is groot. → ___ is groot.

a: Zij komt uit Antwerpen
Ze komt uit Antwerpen
Zij is uit Antwerpen
Ze is uit Antwerpen
items.e: komen uit = to come from. Antwerpen = Antwerp.

items.q: In informal spoken Flemish, instead of 'jij' you often hear:

a: jij
items.e: For a contrast you use the stressed form jij.

a: Jullie zijn moe

items.q: Which pronoun is both singular and plural?
items.e: u works for one person or several.

4.t: The book is new. → It's new.

g.hij: he / it (also for things with de)

5.t: The table is big. → It's big.

g.du: you in German, not in Dutch

9.t: YOU are my friend, not him!

hard.q: «Mevrouw Peeters, ___ bent nieuw in Gent, toch?»
hard.e: With mevrouw (a lady you don't know well) you use the polite u, with the jij form of the verb: u bent. jij has the right verb form but is too familiar.
hard.tt: Mrs. Peeters, you're new in Ghent, aren't you?

hard.q: Het boek en de tafel zijn nieuw. → ___ zijn nieuw.
hard.e: For several things it's always ze, whatever the article: a het-word plus a de-word still gives ze.

g.ze: they (also for things in the plural)

hard.tt: The book and the table are new. → They're new.

hard.q: Anna en ik komen uit Italië, maar ___ wonen nu in Antwerpen.
a: we
wij
hard.e: Anna + I = we: we or wij, with a plural verb (wonen). Don't be fooled by Anna en ik: the right pronoun is neither ik nor ze.
hard.tt: Anna and I come from Italy, but now we live in Antwerp.

hard.q: Meneer Claes, ___ u ook uit Brussel?
a: bent
hard.e: With u, zijn works like with jij: u bent, never u is.
hard.tt: Mr. Claes, are you from Brussels too?

hard.q: You guys live in Bruges, but we live in Ghent.
a: Jullie wonen in Brugge, maar wij wonen in Gent
Jullie wonen in Brugge, maar we wonen in Gent
Jullie wonen in Brugge maar wij wonen in Gent
Jullie wonen in Brugge maar we wonen in Gent
hard.e: jullie and wij take the plural verb: wonen. With a contrast the stressed wij sounds best. Brugge = Bruges.

hard.q: She (Anna) is my friend and lives in Ghent.
a: Zij is mijn vriendin en ze woont in Gent
Zij is mijn vriendin en zij woont in Gent
Ze is mijn vriendin en ze woont in Gent
Ze is mijn vriendin en zij woont in Gent
Zij is mijn vriendin en woont in Gent
Ze is mijn vriendin en woont in Gent
hard.e: zij/ze + is (singular) = she. After en you can repeat the pronoun or leave it out, as in English, because the subject is the same.

hard.q: He lives in Bruges, but she comes from Antwerp.
hard.a: Hij woont in Brugge maar ze komt uit Antwerpen
hard.e: Two clauses, each with its own subject: hij woont … ze komt uit. Both verbs stay singular.
hard.tt: He lives in Bruges, but she comes from Antwerp.

hard.q: You guys are tired, but we aren't.
hard.a: Jullie zijn moe maar wij niet
hard.e: jullie zijn (plural). In the contrast maar wij niet the person is stressed, so you need the strong form wij: maar we niet is wrong.
hard.tt: You guys are tired, but we aren't.
